summary: This is Snowflake documentation for the SHOW MODELS command, which lists the machine learning models a user has privileges to access. Results include table metadata and properties, ordered by database, schema, and model name. The page covers the syntax, the LIKE and IN DATABASE/SCHEMA parameters with their default scoping rules, the output columns, and usage notes about pagination when results span multiple schemas.
one_line: Snowflake SHOW MODELS command: syntax, parameters, scope rules, output columns, and pagination notes for listing ML models.
key_facts: SHOW MODELS is available to all Snowflake accounts.
SHOW MODELS lists the machine learning models that the user has privileges to access.
Output is ordered lexicographically by database, schema, and model name.
The syntax is SHOW MODELS [ LIKE '<pattern>' ] [ IN { DATABASE [ <db_name> ] | SCHEMA [ <schema_name> ] } ].
The LIKE filter uses case-insensitive pattern matching with SQL wildcards % and _.
The keyword ACCOUNT retrieves records for all schemas in all databases of the current account.
If there is no current database and DATABASE is specified without a name, the command retrieves records for all databases and schemas in the account.
The default scope is DATABASE when the session has a database in use, and account scope when it has no database.
The output columns are created_on, name, database_name, schema_name, owner, comment, versions, and default_version_name.
The versions column is a JSON array listing versions of the model.
default_version_name is the version used when referring to the model without a version.
Results sorted by database, schema, then model name can break pagination when a database contains models from multiple schemas.
To make pagination work as expected, execute SHOW MODELS for a single schema, using IN SCHEMA schema_name or USE SCHEMA first.
Unqualified schema names with no current database produce the error 'SQL compilation error: Object does not exist, or operation cannot be performed'.
